newsitem.title: UK: Brazil telecoms shine,comsumers pale for LatInvest.
newsitem.headline: Brazil telecoms shine,comsumers pale for LatInvest.

text.p: Latin American brokerage BBV LatInvest said on Friday Brazilian consumer firms Brasmotor and Multibras were unattractive assets while good value was to be found in the country's telecom sector.

"Brazilian white goods manufacturer Brasmotor and subsidiary Multibras are unattractive investments, despite excellent 1996 results and cheap 1996 valuations," BBV LatInvest analyst Liza Perkins said in a statement released in London.
"We recommend Sell Multibras down to R$1.05," she said. "For Brasmotor, however, the bad news is already reflected in the share price...We rate Brasmotor a Hold at R$281."

Perkins said the Brasmotor group would experience falling profits and cash generation in 1997 and 1998 as increased competition exerts downward pressure on prices, while capital expenditure and advertising expenses rise.
Slowing demand, the expected introduction of consumer credit restrictions and a recovery in the cost of raw materials will exacerbate those effects, she added.
"As a result, most valuations will double by 1998," she said.

Telecoms analyst Patrick Grenham said Brazil's Telebras, Telesp and Telepar were BBV LatInvest's favourite sector picks, following the sale earlier this week of 35 percent of the voting capital of Rio Grande do Sul state's telephone operator CRT.
"The Telebras companies still offer substantial value compared to the minimum privatisation values that the Brazilian government is likely to demand," Grenham said.
He said the risks associated with the firms, related to likely governmental actions in setting up a regulatory framework, were more than discounted in their valuations at current prices.
Brazil's telecoms sector forms a key part of a major privatisation drive as the government gears up to dismantle Latin America's largest phone company Telebras during 1997.
Grenham favoured Telebras PN because through it investors gain exposure to its long distance unit Embratel and to part of the country's cellular network.
Telesp PN was also a favourite since it is expected to be the first company on the privatisation block in 1997, and any introduction of a flat access tariff regime would benefit its cash flows.

Telepar is also on his recommended buy list. He said its share price was cheap relative to the sector, more than discounting the risk that existing shareholders could lose out in the forthcoming merger of Telepar with other phone companies in Brazil's south. --Caroline Brothers, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
